title: Capstone Part 3 - Deploy, Scale, Secure, and Monitor
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Capstone Part 3 — Deploy, Scale, Secure, and Monitor ##### The load test that found the real ceiling A team was confident their platform would handle peak volume. The architecture said 15,000 events a day, the workers were horizontally scalable, and everything passed functional tests. The first load test broke at 40 concurrent requests — nowhere near the target. The bottleneck was not compute, not the queue, and not the AI service. It was **PostgreSQL connections**: four workers × a pool of 20, plus the API's pool, plus n8n's, added up past `max_connections=100`. New connections were refused, workers crashed, and the queue backed up. The fix was PgBouncer and smaller pools — twenty minutes of work. Finding it required actually applying load, because nothing in the design document predicted it. Part 3 is where the capstone becomes a system you can operate: deployed reproducibly, secured properly, resilient by design, observable in production, and **proven at target volume** rather than assumed. ##### Containerize and deploy Multi-stage, non-root images per service, and a Compose stack for the full local and small-production footprint: ```yaml services: postgres: image: postgres:16-alpine command: ["postgres", "-c", "max_connections=200", "-c", "shared_buffers=1GB"] volumes: [pg_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data] healthcheck: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $${POSTGRES_USER}"] interval: 10s networks: [backend] pgbouncer: # the fix from the story above image: edoburu/pgbouncer:latest environment: DB_HOST: postgres POOL_MODE: transaction MAX_CLIENT_CONN: 500 DEFAULT_POOL_SIZE: 25 depends_on: { postgres: { condition: service_healthy } } networks: [backend] ingestion: image: ghcr.io/acme/ingestion:${VERSION} environment: DATABASE_URL: postgresql://app@pgbouncer:5432/platform VAULT_ADDR: http://vault:8200 deploy: { replicas: 2, resources: { limits: { memory: 512M } } } healthcheck: test: ["CMD", "curl", "-fsS", "http://localhost:8000/healthz/ready"] start_period: 20s networks: [backend, frontend] n8n-worker: image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:1.80.0 command: worker --concurrency=8 environment: EXECUTIONS_MODE: queue QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_HOST: redis DB_POSTGRESDB_HOST: pgbouncer N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY: ${N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY} deploy: { replicas: 3 } networks: [backend] ``` For Kubernetes deployments, the same shape becomes Deployments with readiness and liveness probes, an HPA on the API, and **KEDA scaling workers on Redis queue depth** — the correct signal for I/O-bound automation work, as CPU stays near-idle while a backlog grows. ##### Terraform-provisioned infrastructure Everything the stack runs on, declared and reviewable: ```hcl module "platform" { source = "../../modules/automation-platform" environment = "prod" region = "ap-south-1" # data residency requirement from Part 1 instance_size = "s-4vcpu-8gb" db_size = "db-s-2vcpu-4gb" db_nodes = 2 # primary + standby worker_count = 3 domain = "automation.acme.in" } resource "digitalocean_database_firewall" "pg" { cluster_id = module.platform.database_id rule { type = "droplet" value = module.platform.app_droplet_id } # No public access rule — the database is unreachable from the internet } ``` With remote state in S3 plus DynamoDB locking, and staging built from the same module with smaller parameters — which is what makes staging a genuine rehearsal rather than an approximation. ##### CI/CD with a gated production deploy ```yaml jobs: test: # lint → mypy → pytest (real Postgres + Redis services) → LLM eval set build: needs: test # multi-stage build, tag with commit SHA, push to registry migrate: needs: build environment: production # run Alembic as a SEPARATE job before deploy — never on app startup, # or N replicas race to migrate the same schema steps: - run: alembic upgrade head deploy: needs: migrate environment: production # required-reviewer gate lives here steps: - run: | kubectl set image deployment/ingestion \ api=ghcr.io/acme/ingestion:${{ github.sha }} kubectl rollout status deployment/ingestion --timeout=300s - name: Smoke test or roll back run: | if ! curl -fsS --retry 6 --retry-delay 5 https://automation.acme.in/healthz/ready; then kubectl rollout undo deployment/ingestion exit 1 fi ``` Two details worth carrying into any production pipeline: **migrations as their own job** before deployment, and an **automatic rollback** when the post-deploy smoke test fails. ##### Secrets and rotation Runtime retrieval via workload identity, so nothing is baked into images or environment files: ```python @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1) def vault_client() -> hvac.Client: c = hvac.Client(url=os.environ["VAULT_ADDR"]) c.auth.kubernetes.login( # pod identity solves secret-zero role="automation-platform", jwt=Path("/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token").read_text(), ) return c class SecretCache: """TTL cache so rotation propagates without a redeploy.""" def __init__(self, ttl: int = 300): self._ttl, self._store = ttl, {} async def get(self, path: str, key: str) -> str: now = time.monotonic() cached = self._store.get((path, key)) if cached and now - cached[1] < self._ttl: return cached[0] value = vault_client().secrets.kv.v2.read_secret_version( path=path)["data"]["data"][key] self._store[(path, key)] = (value, now) return value ``` That TTL cache is what makes rotation operationally real: rotate a credential in Vault and every service picks it up within five minutes, with no deploy and no downtime. Dynamic database credentials with a one-hour TTL go further — a leaked credential expires on its own. ##### Resilience wired in Each pattern from Day 34, applied at a specific place in the pipeline: ```python BREAKERS = { "crm": CircuitBreaker("crm", failure_threshold=5, recovery_timeout=30), "enrich": CircuitBreaker("enrich", failure_threshold=3, recovery_timeout=60), "llm": CircuitBreaker("llm", failure_threshold=5, recovery_timeout=20), } async def call_crm(payload: dict) -> dict: try: return await BREAKERS["crm"].call(crm_client.upsert, payload) except CircuitOpenError: await queue_for_later(payload, reason="crm_circuit_open") # graceful degradation return {"deferred": True} ``` The full set in place before go-live: **idempotency** on every write (unique constraints plus `ON CONFLICT`), **retries** with exponential backoff and jitter on transient failures only, **circuit breakers** with fallbacks per external dependency, a **dead-letter table** with alerting and a replay command, **bulkheads** bounding concurrency per dependency, and **saga compensation** for the multi-step order flow. Then test each one deliberately. Point the CRM URL at a black hole and confirm the breaker opens, the fallback queues, and the alert fires. ##### Observability ```python # Metrics — low-cardinality labels only EVENTS = Counter("platform_events_total", "Events", ["source", "outcome"]) LATENCY = Histogram("platform_e2e_seconds", "Webhook to completion", ["source"], buckets=(0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 300)) QUEUE = Gauge("platform_queue_depth", "Pending", ["queue"]) AI_COST = Counter("platform_ai_cost_usd", "LLM spend", ["tenant", "workflow"]) # Traces — high-cardinality attributes belong here with tracer.start_as_current_span("process_event") as span: span.set_attribute("event.id", event_id) span.set_attribute("tenant.id", tenant_id) # Logs — structured, with the trace ID bound structlog.contextvars.bind_contextvars(trace_id=trace_id, tenant=tenant_id) ``` The Grafana dashboard's top row should answer "is anything wrong?" in three seconds: success rate against the SLO line, p95 end-to-end latency, queue depth, and DLQ count. Below that, per-source breakdowns, third-party error rates, and AI cost per tenant. **Langfuse** traces every LLM call so prompt-level quality and cost sit alongside infrastructure metrics. The four alerts that matter: ```yaml - alert: SLOBreach expr: (sum(rate(platform_events_total{outcome="success"}[15m])) / sum(rate(platform_events_total[15m]))) < 0.995 for: 10m labels: { severity: critical } annotations: { runbook: "https://wiki/runbooks/slo-breach" } - alert: NoEventsReceived # the silent-failure detector expr: sum(rate(platform_events_total[30m])) == 0 for: 30m labels: { severity: critical } - alert: QueueBacklogGrowing expr: platform_queue_depth > 500 and deriv(platform_queue_depth[10m]) > 0 for: 15m - alert: DeadLetterGrowth expr: increase(platform_dead_letters_total[1h]) > 20 ``` ##### Load testing and tuning ```javascript // k6: ramp to target, then beyond, to find the ceiling export const options = { stages: [ { duration: '2m', target: 20 }, { duration: '5m', target: 50 }, // ~15,000/day equivalent { duration: '3m', target: 150 }, // 3x peak — find the breaking point { duration: '2m', target: 0 }, ], thresholds: { http_req_duration: ['p(95)<200'], // fast-ack requirement from Part 1 http_req_failed: ['rate<0.005'], }, }; export default function () { const res = http.post(`${__ENV.TARGET}/v1/webhooks/shopify`, buildPayload(), { headers: { 'X-Shopify-Hmac-Sha256': sign(payload) }, }); check(res, { 'accepted': (r) => r.status === 202, 'fast ack': (r) => r.timings.duration < 200 }); } ``` Watch the dashboard while it runs and record **what saturates first**. The usual candidates, in the order teams actually hit them: 1. **Database connections** — the opening story. Fix with PgBouncer in transaction mode and smaller per-process pools. 2. **Worker concurrency** — queue depth grows while CPU stays low; add workers or raise concurrency. 3. **External rate limits** — 429s appear; add throttling and a circuit breaker. 4. **AI latency and cost** — p95 balloons; add caching and route simple cases to a small model. 5. **Memory** — OOMKills under large payloads; set limits and stream large bodies. Then re-test after each fix, one change at a time, so you can attribute the improvement. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[k6 load test
ramp to 3x peak] --> B[Watch Grafana:
what saturates?] B --> C{Bottleneck} C -->|DB connections| D[PgBouncer + smaller pools] C -->|queue depth| E[More workers / KEDA] C -->|429s| F[Throttle + circuit breaker] C -->|AI p95| G[Cache + model routing] C -->|OOM| H[Limits + streaming] D & E & F & G & H --> I[Re-test] I --> J{Thresholds met
at target volume?} J -->|no| A J -->|yes| K[Record capacity ceiling
+ headroom in runbook] ``` ##### Common pitfalls - **Load testing only at target volume** — you learn nothing about the ceiling or the failure mode. - **Connection exhaustion** from unpooled workers; count `replicas × pool_size` against `max_connections`. - **Migrations on application startup**, so replicas race. - **Autoscaling workers on CPU** rather than queue depth. - **Liveness probes that check the database**, converting a blip into a mass restart. - **Untested alerts** — break something on purpose before you rely on them. - **No automatic rollback** on a failed smoke test. - **Secrets fetched once at boot**, so rotation requires a redeploy. - **High-cardinality Prometheus labels** taking the metrics stack down. - **No capacity number recorded**, so nobody knows the safe operating limit. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: **deploy the capstone to production via CI/CD** with Terraform-provisioned infrastructure, Vault secrets, resilience patterns, and a live Grafana dashboard plus alerts — then **load-test at target volume**. Do the cutover carefully: shadow run, then limited scope, then full, with the rollback command written down before you need it. The mini project is that deployment made complete and operable. Verify each control rather than assuming it: revoke a credential and watch the alert; kill a worker mid-run and confirm the event reprocesses; point a dependency at a dead host and watch the circuit open and the fallback engage. For the assignment, **run a load test at target volume and prove autoscaling and alerting behave correctly under stress**. Report the numbers: throughput achieved, p95 at target and at 3× target, what saturated first, what you changed, and the improvement. Include the **capacity ceiling** you measured and the headroom it gives you against projected growth — that number belongs in the runbook, and being able to state it is what distinguishes a deployed system from an operated one. ##### Key takeaways - Deploy from Terraform-provisioned infrastructure through a gated CI/CD pipeline, with migrations as a separate job and automatic rollback on smoke-test failure. - Fetch secrets at runtime with workload identity and a TTL cache so rotation propagates without a redeploy; prefer short-lived dynamic credentials. - Wire idempotency, retries, circuit breakers with fallbacks, dead-lettering and bulkheads before go-live, then test each by deliberately causing the failure. - Instrument metrics, traces and structured logs sharing a trace ID, and ship four alerts: SLO breach, no traffic, queue backlog, and dead-letter growth. - Load test past your target to find the real ceiling — usually database connections first — fix one thing at a time, and record the measured capacity in the runbook.
